sections.title: A machine made only of switches
sections.intro_md:
In March 2025 Apple announced a chip, the M3 Ultra, with **184 billion transistors** on it. The Population Reference Bureau estimates that about **117 billion** humans have ever been born. One chip in a desktop computer now holds more tiny switches than there have ever been people.

Every one of those transistors does one dull thing: it is either on or off. That is the whole trick, and it is the paradox of today. Nothing inside a computer understands a photo, a song or a sentence. There are only switches, and switches that flip other switches, billions of times a second.

Eighty years ago the word "computer" meant a person, usually a woman with a pencil. Today you will follow the line from those people, through brass gears, telephone relays, glowing valves and grains of purified sand, to the software on your phone. By the end you should be able to explain, in plain words, what actually happens between pressing a key and seeing a letter appear.

spotlights.name: ENIAC, the 27-tonne calculator

where.label: Moore School of Electrical Engineering, Philadelphia

spotlights.spot_it: A U-shaped wall of black panels, dials and patch cables filling a room in Philadelphia, with people plugging wires like a telephone exchange.
spotlights.story_md: The US Army paid the University of Pennsylvania to build ENIAC to compute artillery firing tables. John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert's team used **17,468 vacuum tubes**, about 70,000 resistors and some 5 million hand-soldered joints. It weighed about **27 tonnes**, filled roughly 167 square metres and drew **150 kilowatts**. It could add 5,000 numbers a second, which made it about a thousand times faster than the relay machines before it. The catch: there was no stored program. To change the problem, people rewired it with cables and switches, which could take days. Tubes burned out often, so engineers learned to leave it running.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved that electronic switching could do general-purpose maths at a speed no human team could match.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thirty tonnes, 17,468 glowing tubes, and reprogrammed by pulling cables.

spotlights.name: The six women who programmed ENIAC
spotlights.spot_it: Black and white photos of young women at ENIAC's plugboards, often printed for decades with no names in the caption.
spotlights.story_md: Kathleen McNulty, Jean Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Frances Bilas and Ruth Lichterman were hired as human computers and picked to program ENIAC. At first they were not cleared to see the machine, so they learned it from its wiring diagrams. They worked out how to break a ballistics problem into steps the hardware could do, then set thousands of switches and cables by hand. At the public unveiling in February 1946 their trajectory program ran perfectly, yet the press coverage and the celebration dinner left them out. When researcher Kathy Kleiman found the photos in the 1980s, she was told the women were probably models. They were inducted into the Women in Technology International Hall of Fame in 1997.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first programmers of a general-purpose electronic computer were women, and history nearly erased them.
spotlights.memory_hook: Six women learned the machine from its blueprints before they were allowed to touch it.

spotlights.name: When a computer was a person
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of desks, mechanical calculators and women in a 1940s office, with a sign on the door that read Computer Room.
spotlights.story_md: The English word computer is recorded from **1613** for a person who computes. By the late 1800s astronomer Edward Pickering at Harvard hired women, at about 25 to 50 cents an hour, to measure and classify stars on glass photographic plates. One of them, Annie Jump Cannon, classified hundreds of thousands of stars, and Henrietta Leavitt found the rule that let astronomers measure distances to galaxies. In the 1940s and 1950s the US aviation agency NACA, later NASA, ran whole rooms of computers, including the West Area Computers at Langley, where Katherine Johnson and Dorothy Vaughan worked. When electronic machines arrived, the job title moved to the machine.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The machine took its name, and its first programmers, from a human profession.
spotlights.memory_hook: Before it was a box, a computer was a woman with a pencil and a slide rule.

sections.title: What a computer actually is
sections.intro_md:
Strip away the screen and case, and every computer from ENIAC to your phone does four things. It takes **input** (a key, a touch, a sensor), **stores** information in memory, **processes** it by following instructions, and produces **output** (pixels, sound, a signal to a motor).

The idea that made modern computers possible is simple. Put the instructions in the same memory as the data. Then a program is just more numbers, and you load a new one in seconds instead of rewiring a room. This is the **stored-program** design, usually called the von Neumann architecture. It was written up in 1945 and first ran in Manchester in 1948. Almost every computer you have used still follows it.

The rest of today takes those boxes one at a time: the switches that make them, the logic that joins them, the memory that holds state, and the software that drives them. The tiles below give the numbers worth keeping.

spotlights.name: The First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC
spotlights.spot_it: A 101-page typed report, unfinished and full of gaps left for references, with a single name on the cover: John von Neumann.
spotlights.story_md: Von Neumann, a Hungarian-American mathematician working on the atomic bomb, joined discussions with the ENIAC team about their next machine. He wrote up the ideas on train journeys, describing a computer with a processing unit, a control unit, a memory holding both instructions and data, and input and output. Herman Goldstine typed it and circulated it in June 1945 with only von Neumann's name on it. Eckert and Mauchly were furious. The design is still called the **von Neumann architecture**, and because the report counted as publication, it helped wreck their hopes of patenting the stored-program idea.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the blueprint almost every computer since has followed.
spotlights.memory_hook: One report, one name on the cover, and a design named after the man who wrote it down.

spotlights.name: The Manchester Baby runs the first stored program
spotlights.spot_it: Tall grey racks of valves and a small round screen of glowing dots.
spotlights.story_md: Frederic Williams, Tom Kilburn and Geoff Tootill built the Small-Scale Experimental Machine to test a new memory: a cathode-ray tube that held bits as dots of charge on its screen. It stored just **32 words** of 32 bits. On **21 June 1948** it ran a 17-instruction program, written by Kilburn, that found the highest proper factor of 2 to the power 18 by trying every number downwards. It took 52 minutes and about 3.5 million operations, and the answer appeared as dots on the screen. It was the first time a program sat in electronic memory and ran. A working replica was built in 1998 for the 50th anniversary.
spotlights.why_it_matters: From this day, changing what a computer does meant loading numbers, not moving cables.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifty-two minutes to find one factor, and the age of software began.

sections.title: Computing before electricity
sections.intro_md:
Machines that calculate are far older than electricity. They used gears, pins and holes in cards, and each one solved a piece of the puzzle that electronic computers would later put together.

There are two different lineages here. **Analog** machines, like the Antikythera mechanism, model a problem with continuous motion: a gear turns as the Moon moves. **Digital** machines, like Pascal's calculator, count in separate steps: a wheel clicks from 9 to 0 and carries one. Modern computers are digital, but the idea of making a machine *imitate* the world started with the analog ones.

The other thread is **control**. A calculator does one operation when a person turns a crank. A loom in Lyon that read punched cards could follow a long sequence of instructions on its own. Charles Babbage saw that the two ideas could be joined, and Ada Lovelace saw what that would mean. They were a century early. The engineering of the 1830s could not make their machine, and the Science Museum in London only proved the design worked in 1991.

spotlights.name: The Antikythera mechanism
spotlights.spot_it: Corroded green-brown lumps of bronze with tiny triangular gear teeth still visible, in a glass case in Athens.
spotlights.story_md: Sponge divers found a Roman-era shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera in **1900**. Among the statues they raised was a lump of corroded bronze. In 1902 archaeologist Valerios Stais noticed a gear wheel in it. More than a century of X-rays and CT scans has shown about **30 surviving gears** in 82 fragments. Turned by a hand crank, it predicted the positions of the Sun and Moon, the Moon's phase, eclipses years ahead, and the four-year cycle of the Olympic Games. Nothing with gearing this fine survives from the next thousand years. Its date is still argued, from about 205 to 60 BCE.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that the idea of a machine that models the world is more than 2,000 years old.
spotlights.memory_hook: A shoebox of bronze gears that predicted eclipses before Julius Caesar.

spotlights.name: Pascal's calculator

where.label: Musee des Arts et Metiers, Paris

spotlights.spot_it: A polished brass box the size of a shoebox, with a row of small spoked dials on top and number windows above them.
spotlights.story_md: Blaise Pascal was 18 when he started building a calculator to help his father, a tax official in Rouen, with endless sums. Each dial moved a wheel inside, and a clever weighted lever, the **sautoir**, carried a one to the next wheel when a wheel passed from 9 to 0. Pascal made about 50 prototypes and around 20 finished machines over a decade. They were expensive and fiddly, and few sold. Nine survive. The carry is the important part: it is the same problem every adding circuit in a modern chip still has to solve, only now in a billionth of a second.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It mechanised the carry, the core step of all arithmetic hardware.
spotlights.memory_hook: A teenager built it to save his father from tax sums.

spotlights.name: The Jacquard loom and its punched cards
spotlights.spot_it: A tall wooden loom with a long chain of stiff cards, each punched with rows of holes, looping over the top.
spotlights.story_md: Joseph Marie Jacquard's attachment for silk looms in Lyon read a chain of punched cards. Each card was one row of the pattern: where there was a hole, a hook passed through and lifted a thread; where there was none, the thread stayed down. A complex brocade could need thousands of cards, and changing the pattern meant changing the cards, not the loom. Weavers feared for their jobs and attacked some machines. A silk portrait of Jacquard, woven in 1839, took about **24,000 cards**. Charles Babbage owned a copy and showed it to visitors, asking them to guess whether it was an engraving.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the first machine controlled by a stored, swappable sequence of instructions.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hole meant lift, no hole meant stay: the first binary program was a silk pattern.

spotlights.name: Babbage's Difference Engine No. 2
spotlights.spot_it: A gleaming bronze and steel machine about 3.4 metres long, with eight towers of numbered wheels turned by a hand crank.
spotlights.story_md: Charles Babbage wanted to end errors in printed tables of logarithms and navigation, which ships relied on. His difference engines computed tables using only addition, by the method of finite differences. He never finished one. For the 200th anniversary of his birth, the Science Museum in London built **Difference Engine No. 2** from his drawings, completing the calculating section in **1991** and the printer in 2000. It has about 8,000 parts, weighs about 5 tonnes and works to 31 digits. The builders found only small errors in his plans. Half of Babbage's brain is also preserved at the Science Museum.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved a Victorian design for a computing machine was sound.
spotlights.memory_hook: Built 142 years late, and it worked.

spotlights.name: Ada Lovelace and Note G
spotlights.spot_it: A young woman in white in an 1840s watercolour; her fame rests on notes A to G of a translation.
spotlights.story_md: Ada Lovelace, the daughter of the poet Lord Byron, translated an Italian engineer's article on Babbage's planned **Analytical Engine**, a general-purpose machine with a store and a mill. She added notes about three times longer than the article. **Note G** sets out step by step how the engine could compute Bernoulli numbers, often called the first published computer program. More striking was her insight that the machine could act on anything expressed as symbols, even music, not just numbers. She also wrote that it could not originate anything, a line Alan Turing answered a century later as Lady Lovelace's objection. How much of the maths was hers or Babbage's is still debated.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She saw that a computing machine is a symbol machine, not just a calculator.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Engine weaves algebra the way the Jacquard loom weaves flowers.

spotlights.name: Hollerith's census tabulator
spotlights.spot_it: A wooden desk with a press, rows of clock-like dials and a sorting box with lids.
spotlights.story_md: The 1880 US census took about eight years to tabulate by hand, and the population kept growing. Herman Hollerith, an engineer at the Census Office, borrowed the idea of a train conductor punching tickets. Each person became a card with holes in set positions. In his machine, spring-loaded pins pressed down on the card; where there was a hole, a pin dipped into a cup of mercury, closed a circuit and moved a dial on by one. The 1890 census finished far faster and under budget. Hollerith's company merged with others in 1911 and in **1924** was renamed **International Business Machines**: IBM.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the first large-scale use of electricity to process data, and it founded IBM.
spotlights.memory_hook: A hole closed a circuit, a dial clicked, and IBM was born.

sections.title: The idea that logic can be wired
sections.intro_md:
Gears can add. But a modern computer is not really an adding machine. It is a **logic machine**, and the arithmetic is built out of logic.

Three people, working decades apart, made that possible. In 1854 **George Boole** showed that reasoning with true and false could be written as algebra. In 1936 **Alan Turing** showed, on paper, what any mechanical procedure can and cannot do, and that one machine could imitate all others. In 1937 **Claude Shannon** noticed that the on and off of an electrical switch behaves exactly like Boole's true and false.

Put those together and you get the core idea of today: if switches can do logic, and logic can do arithmetic, and one machine can run any procedure, then a big enough pile of switches can do anything that can be computed. What remained was engineering: making the switches faster, smaller and cheaper. That took the rest of the century.

spotlights.name: George Boole's algebra of thought
spotlights.spot_it: A Victorian man with a high collar and side whiskers; his name lives on in every programming language as the word Boolean.
spotlights.story_md: Boole was the son of a shoemaker in Lincoln, England, and largely taught himself mathematics. Though he never earned a degree, he became the first professor of mathematics at Queen's College Cork in Ireland. In **1854** he published *An Investigation of the Laws of Thought*, which treated statements as variables that are either true (1) or false (0), joined by AND, OR and NOT. One of his rules looks strange as ordinary algebra: x times x equals x. In logic it makes sense: true and true is still true. For 80 years this was a curiosity for logicians. He died in 1864 at 49 after walking to a lecture in the rain.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every decision a chip makes is Boolean algebra running in silicon.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Boole's world, x times x is still x.

spotlights.name: Turing's imaginary machine
spotlights.spot_it: Never built, only described: a tape, a head that reads and writes, and a short rule table.
spotlights.story_md: At 24, Alan Turing wrote *On Computable Numbers* to answer a question in logic: is there a mechanical method to decide any mathematical statement? He imagined a person following rules with a pencil and an endless strip of paper, and boiled it down to a machine that reads one symbol, writes one, moves left or right, and changes state. He then showed one such machine, the **universal machine**, could imitate any other if given its description on the tape. That is the idea of software. He also proved some questions, like whether a given program will ever stop, cannot be answered by any machine at all.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It defined what computers can do before any existed, and what they never can.
spotlights.memory_hook: A pencil, a tape, a rule table: the whole of computing on one strip of paper.

spotlights.name: Claude Shannon's master's thesis
spotlights.spot_it: A lean, smiling man who also juggled, rode a unicycle in the corridors of Bell Labs, and built a mechanical mouse that learned a maze.
spotlights.story_md: As a 21-year-old student at MIT, Shannon looked after Vannevar Bush's differential analyzer, a room-sized analog computer controlled by a tangle of relay circuits. He noticed that switches in series behave like AND and switches in parallel behave like OR. His 1937 master's thesis, *A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits*, showed that Boole's algebra could design and simplify any switching circuit on paper, and even add binary numbers. Psychologist Howard Gardner later called it possibly the most important master's thesis of the century. In 1948 Shannon went on to found information theory and popularised the word **bit**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned circuit design from craft into mathematics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two switches in a row are AND; two side by side are OR.

sections.title: The switch, five times over
sections.intro_md:
A computer needs a switch that one electrical signal can flip, so that switches can control other switches. The whole hardware story of the 20th century is the hunt for a better one.

First came the **relay**, a telephone-exchange part: a small electromagnet that pulls a metal contact closed with a click. Reliable, but slow, a few dozen operations a second. Then the **vacuum tube** or valve: a glowing glass bulb where a voltage on a grid lets electrons flow or stops them, with no moving parts, thousands of times faster, but hot and short-lived. Then the **transistor**, a solid crystal that does the same job with no heat to speak of. Then the **integrated circuit**, many transistors made together on one slice. Then the **MOSFET**, the transistor design that could be shrunk again and again.

Each step made the switch smaller, faster, cheaper and more reliable, often by a factor of a thousand. The logic on top barely changed. A NAND gate in 1960 and in 2026 does the same thing.

spotlights.name: Zuse Z3, the relay computer
spotlights.spot_it: Cabinets of clicking telephone relays and a small console with a lamp display, rebuilt in the Deutsches Museum in Munich.
spotlights.story_md: Konrad Zuse, a German civil engineer tired of repetitive stress calculations for aircraft, built his machines in his parents' Berlin flat. The **Z3**, finished in 1941, used about **2,600 relays**, worked in binary with floating-point numbers, and read its program from holes punched in discarded 35 mm film. It did a few additions a second. The German government saw no war use for it. Allied bombing destroyed it in 1943. In 1998 computer scientist Raul Rojas showed that, in principle, it could compute anything a modern machine can, though very awkwardly. A replica built in the 1960s stands in Munich.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the first working programmable, fully automatic digital computer.
spotlights.memory_hook: Programmed on old cinema film, built in a living room.

spotlights.name: Colossus, the secret codebreaker
spotlights.spot_it: Two women in wartime uniform at a tall steel frame of glowing valves, with a loop of paper tape racing over pulleys.
spotlights.story_md: Tommy Flowers, a Post Office telephone engineer, built Colossus to break the Lorenz cipher used by Hitler's high command. Experts told him thousands of valves would be too unreliable; he knew from telephone exchanges that valves rarely fail if left switched on. The Mark 1 ran at Bletchley Park in early 1944 with about **1,600 valves**. The Mark 2, with about 2,400, was working days before D-Day. It read paper tape at **5,000 characters a second**. Ten were built. After the war most were broken up and their existence stayed secret into the 1970s, so Flowers got no public credit for decades. A rebuild runs at The National Museum of Computing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved large electronic machines could be reliable, years before ENIAC.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Post Office engineer won a codebreaking war with 2,400 light bulbs.

spotlights.name: The first transistor

where.label: Bell Labs, Murray Hill, New Jersey

spotlights.spot_it: A plastic triangle wrapped in gold foil, pressed by a bent paperclip spring onto a slab of germanium: crude enough to fit in your palm.
spotlights.story_md: At Bell Labs in New Jersey, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain were trying to replace unreliable valves in the telephone network. In December 1947 Brattain slit gold foil over the tip of a plastic wedge and pushed it into germanium. A small current in one contact controlled a bigger one in the other: the **point-contact transistor**. Their boss William Shockley, stung at being left out, designed a better junction transistor within weeks. The famous 1948 photo of the three shows Shockley sitting at Brattain's apparatus. All three shared the 1956 Nobel Prize. Bardeen later won a second physics Nobel, the only person to do so.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the switch every chip is built from.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gold foil, a paperclip and a lump of germanium started the information age.

spotlights.name: The integrated circuit
spotlights.spot_it: A sliver of germanium smaller than a fingernail glued to glass, with wisps of gold wire looping between its parts.
spotlights.story_md: Wiring thousands of separate transistors by hand created a tangle engineers called the tyranny of numbers. In the summer of 1958 **Jack Kilby**, newly hired at Texas Instruments and without holiday time, worked alone in the empty lab and built a resistor, capacitor and transistor from one piece of germanium. He demonstrated it on 12 September 1958. Months later **Robert Noyce** at Fairchild Semiconductor patented a better way: a flat silicon chip with the connections printed on it in metal, using Jean Hoerni's planar process. Kilby got the 2000 Nobel Prize. Noyce, who co-founded Intel, had died in 1990.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Making all parts at once on one slice is why chips became cheap.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kilby built it because he had no holiday; Noyce made it flat.

spotlights.name: The MOSFET, most-made object in history
spotlights.spot_it: Invisible to the eye: billions of them sit on every chip as tiny gates of metal or polysilicon over a sliver of oxide on silicon.
spotlights.story_md: At Bell Labs in 1959, **Mohamed Atalla**, an Egyptian-born engineer, and **Dawon Kahng**, a Korean-born physicist, built a transistor controlled by a voltage on a gate separated from the silicon by a thin layer of oxide. It was slower than other transistors at first, and Bell Labs paid it little attention. But it used little power and could be made flat and shrunk almost endlessly. Nearly every transistor in every chip since the 1970s is a **MOSFET**. The Computer History Museum cites an estimate that about **13 sextillion**, a 13 followed by 21 zeros, were made between 1960 and 2018.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the switch that scaled, and so the switch the modern world runs on.
spotlights.memory_hook: Humanity has made more MOSFETs than there are stars in the Milky Way, by a factor of tens of billions.

sections.title: Bits: how a switch holds a word, a face, a song
sections.intro_md:
A single switch has two states. Call them 0 and 1 and you have a **bit**. Bits combine fast: 2 bits give 4 patterns, 8 bits give 256, 32 bits about 4.3 billion. Each extra bit doubles the count.

Everything a computer handles becomes patterns like these by agreement. A number is written in base 2: 13 is 1101. A letter is a number from a table: in ASCII, capital A is 65. A colour is three numbers for red, green and blue, each usually 0 to 255, and a photo is a grid of them. A sound is a list of air-pressure readings taken 44,100 or 48,000 times a second.

Nothing in the chip knows which pattern is a letter and which a colour. Meaning comes from the program that reads it, which is why a photo opened in a text editor looks like gibberish. Binary gets its own full day later in the queue.

visual.title: One pattern of bits, many meanings

spotlights.name: The bit
spotlights.spot_it: A woven grid of tiny rings: in old core memory, each ring is one bit.
spotlights.story_md: The word **bit**, short for binary digit, was coined by statistician John Tukey in a 1947 memo and made famous by Claude Shannon's 1948 paper on information. Shannon showed a bit is the amount of information in one fair yes-or-no answer, which is why twenty well-chosen questions can pick one item out of about a million. Inside a chip, a bit is not literally a 1 or 0. It is a voltage, and the circuit treats anything above one threshold as 1 and below another as 0, with a gap between. That safety margin is why digital copies do not degrade the way photocopies do.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the atom of all digital information.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty yes-or-no questions are enough to find one thing in a million.

spotlights.name: ASCII, Unicode and the letter A
spotlights.spot_it: Capital A is 65, which is 01000001 in binary; the Devanagari letter a is code point U+0905.
spotlights.story_md: Early machines each had their own codes for letters, so text from one would not read on another. **ASCII**, agreed in the United States in 1963, used 7 bits for 128 characters: English letters, digits, punctuation and control codes like line feed. It had no room for Hindi, Tamil or Chinese. **Unicode**, first published in 1991, gives every character in every script its own number. Version 17.0, released on 9 September 2025, holds **159,801** characters. The UTF-8 encoding most web pages use was designed by Ken Thompson and Rob Pike in 1992, reportedly sketched on a placemat in a New Jersey diner. It keeps ASCII unchanged and uses up to four bytes for everything else.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is why you can type in Hindi, send an emoji, and have it arrive intact.
spotlights.memory_hook: A is 65 everywhere; अ is U+0905 everywhere.

spotlights.name: The first scanned digital photo
spotlights.spot_it: A grainy black and white square showing a baby's face, made of visible blocks: 176 pixels on each side.
spotlights.story_md: In 1957 Russell Kirsch, a computer scientist at the US National Bureau of Standards, built a drum scanner for SEAC, one of the first stored-program computers in the US. The first picture he fed it was a photo of his three-month-old son, **Walden**. The machine turned it into a grid of **176 by 176** dots, each just black or white, later improved to several shades of grey. That is the birth of the pixel and of image processing: a picture became a table of numbers a program could change. In 2003 *Life* magazine listed it among 100 photographs that changed the world. Kirsch later said he regretted making pixels square.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every digital photo since is the same trick: a picture as a grid of numbers.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first digital photo was a baby, and it had 30,976 pixels.

sections.title: Gates: switches that decide
sections.intro_md:
A **logic gate** is a few transistors wired so the output depends on the inputs in a fixed way. AND outputs 1 only if both inputs are 1. OR outputs 1 if either is. NOT flips its input. **NAND** (NOT AND) outputs 0 only when both inputs are 1.

Gates combine into anything. Two make a **half adder**: XOR gives the sum digit and AND the carry, so 1 + 1 gives sum 0, carry 1, which is binary 10. Chain 64 adders and you can add 64-bit numbers. Loop two gates back into each other and you get a **latch**, which remembers one bit while the power is on. Adders do arithmetic, latches remember, and with those you can build a processor.

The surprise is how little you need. NAND alone is universal: every other gate, and so every computer, can be built from NAND gates and nothing else.

spotlights.name: Stibitz's kitchen-table adder
spotlights.spot_it: Two telephone relays, two flashlight bulbs and strips cut from a tobacco tin, nailed to a board: the K stands for kitchen.
spotlights.story_md: George Stibitz, a mathematician at Bell Labs, took a few discarded relays home in November 1937. On his kitchen table he wired them with flashlight bulbs and switches made from strips of a tobacco tin. Pressing the switches entered two binary digits; the bulbs lit to show the sum in binary. His wife called it the Model K. Bell Labs then let him build the Complex Number Calculator, and in **September 1940** he demonstrated it at a mathematics meeting at Dartmouth College in New Hampshire, while the machine itself sat in New York, linked by a teletype line. That was the first time anyone used a computer remotely.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed binary arithmetic could be done with ordinary telephone parts.
spotlights.memory_hook: Binary addition was born on a kitchen table, lit by flashlight bulbs.

spotlights.name: The NAND gate and the 7400 chip
spotlights.spot_it: A black rectangular chip with 14 metal legs; inside are four NAND gates, the most basic brick of digital logic.
spotlights.story_md: Texas Instruments launched the **7400** family in the 1960s, and the original 7400 chip held four two-input NAND gates. For decades engineers built whole computers by wiring dozens or hundreds of such chips on circuit boards. NAND matters because it is **universal**: wire NAND gates the right way and you get NOT, AND, OR, adders, latches, anything. The Apollo Guidance Computer, which flew men to the Moon, was built from about 2,800 identical chips, each holding two three-input NOR gates, which are universal too. Engineers chose a single chip type because buying one part in bulk made it easier to test and trust.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One gate type is enough to build any computer.
spotlights.memory_hook: Give an engineer enough NAND gates and they can build anything, including a Moon landing.

sections.title: The processor: fetch, decode, execute
sections.intro_md:
The **central processing unit** is a loop that never stops. It **fetches** the next instruction from memory, using a counter that holds its address. It **decodes** it: which operation, which numbers? It **executes** it: the arithmetic logic unit adds, compares or moves bits between **registers**, a handful of very fast storage slots inside the chip. Then it moves the counter on and repeats. A jump instruction changes the counter, which is how a program makes decisions and loops.

Each step is timed by a **clock**, a signal that ticks billions of times a second. At 4 gigahertz, one tick lasts a quarter of a nanosecond, and light itself travels only about 7.5 centimetres in that time. Modern processors cheat the simple picture: they run several instructions at once, guess which way a branch will go, and have many cores side by side. But underneath it is still fetch, decode, execute.

The first time the whole loop fitted on a single chip was 1971. Within a few years microprocessors were in calculators, cash registers, games consoles and, eventually, everything.

spotlights.name: Intel 4004, the first commercial microprocessor
spotlights.spot_it: A cream ceramic package with gold-coloured lid and 16 legs; on the tiny die inside, the designer etched his initials, FF.
spotlights.story_md: A Japanese calculator company, Busicom, asked Intel in 1969 to make a set of custom chips. Intel engineer **Ted Hoff** proposed a simpler plan: one general-purpose processor that software could adapt. **Federico Faggin**, who joined from Fairchild in 1970, did the hard work of designing it in silicon, with Busicom's **Masatoshi Shima** and Intel's Stanley Mazor. The 4004 had **2,300 transistors**, ran at 740 kilohertz and handled 4 bits at a time. Intel bought back the rights from Busicom, which was in trouble, and advertised it in November 1971 as a new era of integrated electronics. It was.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It put a whole processor on one chip and made computers into components.
spotlights.memory_hook: A calculator order from Japan became the first CPU on a chip.

spotlights.name: ARM, the chip that ran on almost nothing
spotlights.spot_it: A small square chip on a green board from Acorn in Cambridge; its descendant is inside nearly every smartphone on Earth.
spotlights.story_md: Acorn, a British home-computer maker, wanted a fast, simple processor and decided to design its own. **Sophie Wilson** wrote the instruction set and **Steve Furber** designed the chip. The first ARM1 came back from the factory on 26 April 1985 and worked first time. During testing they noticed the meter showed no current at all: the chip was running on stray power leaking in through its signal lines. That tiny appetite for power is why ARM designs ended up in phones, where battery life rules. Arm licenses designs rather than making chips, and its partners had shipped more than **200 billion** ARM-based chips by 2021.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Low power, not raw speed, decided who would own the mobile era.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first ARM chip ran with its power supply disconnected.

spotlights.name: The clock and the nanosecond
spotlights.spot_it: A tiny silver can on every circuit board holds a sliver of quartz that vibrates millions of times a second, the heartbeat of the machine.
spotlights.story_md: Squeeze a quartz crystal and it makes a voltage; apply a voltage and it flexes. Cut to the right shape, it rings at a very steady frequency. A watch crystal rings at **32,768 hertz**, which is 2 to the power 15, so halving it 15 times gives exactly one tick a second. Computers start from a crystal and multiply the frequency to several billion ticks a second. Grace Hopper used to hand out pieces of wire about **30 centimetres** long to show admirals a nanosecond: the distance electricity can travel in a billionth of a second. That is why chips are small: at these speeds, distance is delay.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The clock sets the pace of every step, and physics limits how fast it can go.
spotlights.memory_hook: A nanosecond is a foot of wire.

sections.title: Memory: where the switches remember
sections.intro_md:
A processor is useless without somewhere to keep the program and data. Fast memory is expensive and cheap memory is slow, so every computer uses a **hierarchy**.

At the top are **registers** inside the processor, then levels of **cache** on the same chip. Below is **main memory**, or RAM, which forgets everything when the power goes. At the bottom is **storage**, flash or spinning disks, which keeps data with the power off.

The gaps are enormous. If reading the closest cache took one second, reading RAM would take a couple of minutes, a fast SSD hours to a day, and a spinning hard disk months. Much of what makes software fast or slow is whether its data sits near the top of this pyramid. The machines below show how each layer was built, from woven wire to pizza-sized platters to electrons trapped in an insulating cage.

visual.title: How long it takes to reach data (rough, modern PC)

spotlights.name: Magnetic core memory
spotlights.spot_it: A mesh of fine copper wires threaded through thousands of tiny ferrite rings, each smaller than a grain of rice.
spotlights.story_md: Each ring, or core, could be magnetised clockwise or anticlockwise: 1 or 0. Wires crossing through it in a grid let the computer pick any single core by sending half the needed current along one row and half along one column. Only the core at the crossing flipped. MIT's Whirlwind computer used it from 1953, and for about twenty years it was the main memory of almost every computer. It kept its data with the power off. The rings were threaded by hand, often by women working with magnifiers and needles. Programmers still say core dump for the contents of memory when a program crashes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made fast, reliable random-access memory practical for the first time.
spotlights.memory_hook: Each bit was a ring you could see, woven by hand.

spotlights.name: Apollo's woven software
spotlights.spot_it: A sealed metal box with a calculator-like keypad and green number display, the DSKY; inside, the program was literally sewn into wire.
spotlights.story_md: The Apollo Guidance Computer kept its programs in **core rope memory**. A wire threaded through a core meant 1; a wire passing around it meant 0. Women at a Raytheon factory in Massachusetts wove the ropes by hand, guided by machines that pointed to the right hole, and a full set took weeks. Once woven, the software could not be changed, so it had to be right before launch. The computer held about **36,864 words** of rope memory, roughly 72 kilobytes, and 2,048 words of erasable memory. Engineers nicknamed it LOL memory, for the little old ladies who wove it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Software that landed humans on the Moon was hardware, sewn by hand.
spotlights.memory_hook: Wire through the ring is 1, around it is 0: Apollo's code was knitted.

spotlights.name: IBM RAMAC, the first hard disk
spotlights.spot_it: A refrigerator-sized cabinet with a glass window showing a stack of fifty shiny metal platters, each about 60 centimetres across.
spotlights.story_md: Before disks, records lived on tape or cards, and finding one meant reading everything before it. IBM's 350 disk storage unit, sold with the 305 RAMAC computer, let a moving arm jump to any of **fifty 24-inch platters** spinning at 1,200 rpm. It held about **5 million characters**, roughly 3.75 megabytes, weighed about a tonne, and was leased for about 3,200 dollars a month. Moving one meant forklifts and sometimes cargo planes. A microSD card the size of a fingernail now holds hundreds of thousands of times as much. RAMAC stood for Random Access Method of Accounting and Control.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Random access to stored data is what made databases, and so modern business software, possible.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five megabytes, one tonne, fifty platters.

spotlights.name: DRAM: one transistor, one leaky bucket
spotlights.spot_it: The long green sticks of RAM you slot into a laptop or desktop, each covered in black chips holding billions of tiny capacitors.
spotlights.story_md: In 1966 **Robert Dennard** at IBM realised a bit could be stored as a charge on a tiny capacitor, with a single transistor as its door. It was far smaller than earlier memory cells, so far more bits fit on a chip. The catch is that capacitors leak. Every bit must be read and rewritten, or refreshed, many times a second, typically every 64 milliseconds, or the data fades. That is the dynamic in **dynamic RAM**. Intel's 1103 of 1970, holding 1,024 bits, was the first commercial DRAM chip and quickly became the best-selling chip in the world. Modern phones carry many billions of these cells.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Nearly all working memory in computers today is Dennard's cell, copied billions of times.
spotlights.memory_hook: A bucket with a hole, refilled before it empties.

spotlights.name: Flash memory
spotlights.spot_it: The memory in every phone, USB stick and SSD: flat black chips that keep your photos with the power off.
spotlights.story_md: At Toshiba in the early 1980s, engineer **Fujio Masuoka** designed a memory cell that traps electrons on an insulated floating gate, where they can stay for years with no power. Whole blocks could be erased at once; his colleague Shoji Ariizumi said that reminded him of a camera flash, and the name stuck. Toshiba presented NOR flash in 1984 and NAND flash, the dense kind in phones and SSDs, in 1987. Masuoka later said Toshiba gave him a bonus of a few hundred dollars. He sued, and in 2006 the company settled for **87 million yen**, about 758,000 dollars, a fraction of what flash became worth.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It replaced spinning disks in most devices and made phones possible.
spotlights.memory_hook: Erased in a flash, and paid a few hundred dollars for it.

sections.title: Making the chips
sections.intro_md:
In 1965 Gordon Moore noticed that the number of components on the best chips was doubling about every year; in 1975 he revised it to every two years. The industry made his observation come true for half a century, which is why a phone now does what a 1990s supercomputer did.

A chip is made like a print, not like a machine. Pure silicon is grown as a single crystal, sliced into **wafers** 300 millimetres wide and polished flat. Patterns are projected onto the wafer with light, then etched, doped and coated, layer upon layer, in hundreds of steps over about three months. The rooms are kept far cleaner than an operating theatre, because one speck of dust can kill a chip.

The smallest features are now made with **extreme ultraviolet** light. Only one company makes those machines, and most of the most advanced chips come from one company in Taiwan.

spotlights.name: Gordon Moore and his law
spotlights.spot_it: A soft-spoken chemist in large glasses, co-founder of Intel, whose four-page magazine article became the industry's metronome.
spotlights.story_md: Moore, then at Fairchild Semiconductor, was asked by *Electronics* magazine to predict the next ten years. His article, *Cramming more components onto integrated circuits*, plotted just a few data points on a log scale and saw the count doubling yearly. He guessed chips with **65,000** components by 1975, and he was close. Physicist Carver Mead later named it Moore's law. It is not a law of nature but an economic target: companies planned research to hit the next doubling. Moore co-founded Intel with Robert Noyce in 1968 and died on 24 March 2023 at 94.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A forecast became a plan that drove the whole industry for 50 years.
spotlights.memory_hook: Moore's law was a prediction that people made true.

spotlights.name: ASML's extreme ultraviolet machines
spotlights.spot_it: A machine the size of a bus, built in the Netherlands, that fires lasers at falling droplets of tin to make light.
spotlights.story_md: To print features a few nanometres across you need light of very short wavelength. Extreme ultraviolet, at **13.5 nanometres**, is absorbed by air and glass, so the machine works in a vacuum and uses mirrors instead of lenses. It makes the light by hitting tiny droplets of molten tin with a powerful laser, turning each into a glowing plasma. **ASML** of Veldhoven is the only company that makes these machines. Each costs well over 150 million dollars, and ASML says shipping one takes **40 freight containers, 20 trucks and 3 cargo planes**. Without them, no one can make the most advanced chips.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One company's machine is a chokepoint for the whole digital economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Laser hits tin, tin makes light, light prints the chip.

spotlights.name: TSMC, the factory for everyone else's chips
spotlights.spot_it: Huge white fabrication buildings in Hsinchu Science Park, Taiwan; the company's name rarely appears on the products its chips power.
spotlights.story_md: Morris Chang spent 25 years at Texas Instruments before Taiwan's government asked him to build a chip industry. In **1987** he founded the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company with a new business model: it would make no chips of its own design, only manufacture chips designed by others. That let companies like Apple, Nvidia, AMD and Qualcomm design chips without owning factories that cost tens of billions of dollars. TSMC began volume production of its **2 nanometre** process in late 2025, with Apple reported to have taken about half of early capacity. The name 2 nm is a label; no feature on the chip is actually 2 nm wide.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Much of the world's most advanced computing depends on factories on one island.
spotlights.memory_hook: TSMC makes the chips; other people's logos go on them.

sections.title: Software: words that become switches
sections.intro_md:
The processor only understands **machine code**: numbers that mean things like add register 1 to register 2. Early programmers wrote those numbers directly or set them with switches, and every program today is still turned into machine code before it runs.

The history of software is a history of layers that let people say more with less. **Assembly language** gave each instruction a short name like ADD. **Compilers** translated something close to English or algebra into machine code automatically. **Operating systems** took over the jobs every program needs, such as files, memory and the screen. Libraries, frameworks and now AI coding tools sit on top.

Each layer was resisted at first. Engineers doubted a compiler could match a human, or that an operating system could be written in a high-level language. The people below proved them wrong.

spotlights.name: Grace Hopper and the compiler
spotlights.spot_it: A slight woman in a US Navy uniform with a wry smile, who handed out pieces of wire to explain nanoseconds.
spotlights.story_md: Grace Hopper earned a mathematics PhD from Yale in 1934, joined the US Navy in 1943 and programmed the Harvard Mark I. Working on UNIVAC in **1952**, she wrote the A-0 system, an early compiler that assembled programs from stored routines. Colleagues told her computers could only do arithmetic, not understand words. She built FLOW-MATIC, which used English-like commands, and it shaped **COBOL** in 1959, a language still running many bank and government systems. She retired from the Navy at 79 as a rear admiral, the oldest serving officer. She liked to say it is easier to ask forgiveness than to get permission.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She made programming a matter of writing language, not numbers.
spotlights.memory_hook: Told computers only did arithmetic, she taught them English.

spotlights.name: FORTRAN, the first widely used high-level language
spotlights.spot_it: A punched card with one line of code printed on top: a program was a deck of these.
spotlights.story_md: John Backus at IBM proposed in 1953 a way to write maths like algebra and let the machine produce the code. He later said much of his work came from being lazy and not liking to write programs. His small team spent about three years on the compiler for the IBM 704. The big doubt was speed: if the code it produced was slow, scientists would not use it. So they worked hard on optimisation, and FORTRAN code ran nearly as fast as hand-written code. It spread through science and engineering within a few years. Versions of Fortran still run weather and climate models today.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved compilers could beat the cost of writing machine code by hand.
spotlights.memory_hook: One line of code, one punched card.

spotlights.name: Unix and C
spotlights.spot_it: Two bearded men at a teletype terminal beside a cabinet-sized minicomputer at Bell Labs.
spotlights.story_md: When Bell Labs pulled out of a large operating system project in 1969, **Ken Thompson** wrote a small one of his own on a little-used PDP-7 minicomputer. **Dennis Ritchie** created the **C** language in 1972, and in 1973 they rewrote Unix in C. That was the breakthrough: an operating system written in a high-level language could be moved to new hardware by recompiling it. Unix's ideas, small tools that do one thing and pass text to each other, shaped macOS, iOS, Android and the servers behind the internet. Unix counts time in seconds from **1 January 1970**, and a 32-bit counter of that runs out on 19 January 2038.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Most of the world's devices run descendants of Unix or Unix ideas.
spotlights.memory_hook: Time began on 1 January 1970, at least for computers.

spotlights.name: Linux, the hobby that took over
spotlights.spot_it: A cheerful cartoon penguin called Tux, the mascot of a kernel that runs Android phones and every one of the world's 500 fastest supercomputers.
spotlights.story_md: Linus Torvalds, a 21-year-old student at the University of Helsinki, posted to an online newsgroup in August 1991 that he was writing a free operating system, adding that it was just a hobby and would not be big and professional. He released the code, and thousands of volunteers and companies improved it. Linux is the **kernel**: the core program that manages memory, processes and hardware. It powers Android, most web servers, and since November 2017 every system on the TOP500 list of supercomputers. In 2005 Torvalds also wrote Git, the tool most programmers use to track code changes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Free, shared software became the foundation of the internet and of phones.
spotlights.memory_hook: Just a hobby, he said, and it now runs 500 of 500 supercomputers.

spotlights.name: Margaret Hamilton and the Apollo 11 alarms
spotlights.spot_it: A young woman standing next to a stack of printed program listings as tall as she is, the Apollo flight software.
spotlights.story_md: Margaret Hamilton led the team at MIT that wrote the onboard flight software for Apollo. Minutes before the first Moon landing, the computer flashed **1202** and **1201** alarms: it was overloaded, partly because a radar was sending it unneeded work. Because the software ran tasks by priority, it dropped the low-priority jobs, restarted and kept the vital landing calculations going. Mission control said go. Hamilton pushed for the term **software engineering** so code would be taken as seriously as hardware. She received the US Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Good design under failure saved the first Moon landing.
spotlights.memory_hook: The computer said 1202, dropped what did not matter, and landed.

sections.title: From power button to a letter on screen
sections.intro_md:
Here is the whole stack at work. Press the power button. The processor wakes and fetches instructions from a fixed address that points into a small **firmware** chip on the main board (BIOS on older PCs, UEFI on newer ones). That code tests the hardware, finds the drive and loads a **bootloader**, which loads the **operating system kernel**. The kernel starts drivers for the screen, keyboard and network, then the programs you see. Boot comes from pulling yourself up by your own bootstraps.

Now press A. A switch under the key closes a circuit in a grid of wires. A tiny processor in the keyboard notices which crossing closed, waits out the bouncing of the contacts and sends a code over USB. The operating system turns it into a character and hands it to the app. A font file describes the shape of A as curves, the graphics processor fills in the pixels, and the screen redraws, 60 to 120 times a second. All in a few hundredths of a second.

spotlights.name: Firmware: the first code that runs
spotlights.spot_it: A small chip on the motherboard, often near a coin-shaped battery, holding the code that runs before any operating system.
spotlights.story_md: When a computer is switched on, its memory is empty, and its processor knows only one thing: where to look first. That address points to **firmware** stored on a flash chip on the board. The name **BIOS**, for basic input/output system, was coined by Gary Kildall in 1975 for his CP/M operating system and became standard with the IBM PC in 1981. It runs a power-on self-test, the beep many older PCs made when everything was fine, then hands control to the bootloader. Modern PCs use **UEFI**, which can check that the operating system has not been tampered with before running it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It solves the chicken-and-egg problem of a computer that needs software to load software.
spotlights.memory_hook: A computer wakes up knowing exactly one address.

spotlights.name: The keypress and the USB cable
spotlights.spot_it: A keyboard switch under every key, a small stem and spring; and the rectangular USB plug that took three tries to insert.
spotlights.story_md: Under each key is a switch at the crossing of a row wire and a column wire. The keyboard's own little processor scans the grid many times a second to see which crossings are closed, ignores the few milliseconds of electrical chatter as the metal contacts bounce, then sends a code to the computer. That code travels over **USB**, a standard developed from 1994 by a group of companies led by Intel. **Ajay Bhatt**, an Indian-born Intel engineer who studied at the Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, was a key architect. USB was made royalty-free, so he earned nothing per plug, but Intel made him a star of a 2009 TV advert.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The humble cable that ended the mess of different ports was co-designed by an engineer from Vadodara.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every plug-in device you own owes something to a Baroda graduate.

spotlights.name: The graphics processor
spotlights.spot_it: A large circuit board with fans and a heat sink, holding a chip made of thousands of small, simple cores working in parallel.
spotlights.story_md: A screen of 1920 by 1080 pixels has about 2 million dots, each needing its colour worked out 60 or more times a second. A CPU has a few powerful cores; a **GPU** has thousands of simpler ones that all run the same small program on different pixels at once. Nvidia marketed its GeForce 256 in 1999 as the world's first GPU. Researchers then found that training neural networks is the same kind of massively parallel arithmetic. In 2012 a network called AlexNet, trained on two Nvidia gaming cards, won a major image-recognition contest. That set off the AI boom, and on 29 October 2025 Nvidia became the first company valued at **5 trillion dollars**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Hardware built for video games became the engine of modern AI.
spotlights.memory_hook: Built to paint pixels for games, it now trains AI.

sections.title: India and the computer
sections.intro_md:
India's computing history started early, then took detours. In 1953 the **Indian Statistical Institute** in Kolkata built an analog computer from war-surplus parts, and in 1955 to 1956 it installed the first digital computer in India. At the **Tata Institute of Fundamental Research** in Mumbai, Homi Bhabha backed a team that built India's own, TIFRAC, by 1960.

Then came decades of import licences and protected public-sector firms. MIT historian Dwai Banerjee's 2026 book calls it the tech revolution that wasn't. When the United States refused to sell India a Cray in 1987, the answer was PARAM. India's real strength became software services, from TCS in 1968 onward, while Indian-born engineers such as Vinod Dham, often called the father of the Pentium, and Ajay Bhatt of USB shaped global hardware.

Now India is trying again with chips: open processor designs, ISRO's space-grade processors, and from 2026 the first plants that assemble and test memory chips at home.

spotlights.name: ISI Kolkata and India's first computers
spotlights.spot_it: The red-brick campus of the Indian Statistical Institute in Baranagar, Kolkata, where P. C. Mahalanobis brought computing to India.
spotlights.story_md: Statistician **P. C. Mahalanobis** needed to crunch huge survey data for planning. At his Indian Statistical Institute, **Samarendra Kumar Mitra**'s team built an analog computer in 1953 from parts salvaged from war-disposal markets in Kolkata; it could solve sets of linear equations. In 1955 to 1956 the institute installed the **HEC-2M**, a British-built digital machine with a magnetic drum memory of 1,024 words, paid for with help from the Soviet Union and the United Nations. In 1966 ISI and Jadavpur University completed **ISIJU-1**, India's first transistorised computer. The early lead came from a statistics institute, not an engineering college.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's computing began as a tool for national planning.
spotlights.memory_hook: India's first computer was built from war junk to solve survey sums.

spotlights.name: TIFRAC, India's first home-built computer

where.label: Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Mumbai

spotlights.spot_it: A 1960s photograph of Jawaharlal Nehru at a cabinet of electronics in Mumbai, being shown the machine he named.
spotlights.story_md: Homi Bhabha's Tata Institute of Fundamental Research decided in the mid-1950s to build a computer rather than buy one, to train engineers. A team led by **R. Narasimhan** based it on the IAS machine design from Princeton, built a pilot in 1956, and had the full machine running by **1960**, after air-conditioning trouble delayed it. It used vacuum tubes and magnetic core memory and served scientists until the mid-1960s. Jawaharlal Nehru named it TIFRAC, the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research Automatic Calculator. Sources disagree on when: at the 1960 commissioning, or on a visit in January 1962.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed Indian engineers could design and build a full computer in the 1950s.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nehru gave India's first computer its name.

spotlights.name: PARAM, the supercomputer born of a refusal
spotlights.spot_it: Racks of processor boards at C-DAC in Pune, under a name that means supreme in Sanskrit.
spotlights.story_md: In 1987 India asked to buy a Cray supercomputer for weather forecasting. The United States, worried it could be used for nuclear weapons work, blocked the sale. India set up the **Centre for Development of Advanced Computing** (C-DAC) in Pune in 1988 under **Vijay Bhatkar**, with a three-year deadline and a budget of about 30 crore rupees, roughly what a Cray would have cost. Its answer, **PARAM 8000**, came out in 1991 built from many processors working in parallel. India later exported PARAM machines. The series continues: PARAM Rudra systems were unveiled in 2024 under the National Supercomputing Mission.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Being refused technology pushed India to build its own.
spotlights.memory_hook: Denied a Cray, India built a PARAM.

spotlights.name: SHAKTI, an open Indian processor
spotlights.spot_it: A small IIT Madras chip built on RISC-V, an instruction set anyone can use free.
spotlights.story_md: Processor designs like x86 and ARM are owned by companies and need licences. **RISC-V** is an open instruction set from the University of California, Berkeley. In 2016 a team at **IIT Madras** led by V. Kamakoti began SHAKTI, a family of RISC-V processors. A test chip was made in 2018 at Intel's factory in Oregon, and in 2020 the Moushik chip was fabricated at the Semiconductor Laboratory in Mohali. The aim is processors India can design, audit and modify itself, for defence, power grids and sensors, without depending on a foreign licence.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Open designs give a country without legacy chip firms a way in.
spotlights.memory_hook: Shakti means strength; the design is free for anyone.

spotlights.name: Vikram 3201, ISRO's 32-bit processor
spotlights.spot_it: A small ceramic-packaged chip billed in 2025 as India's first fully indigenous 32-bit microprocessor.
spotlights.story_md: ISRO's **Semiconductor Laboratory** in Mohali designed and made Vikram 3201 to run navigation and control in launch vehicles. It succeeds the 16-bit Vikram 1601 that has flown in Indian rockets since 2009. It works from minus 55 to plus 125 degrees Celsius and was tested in orbit aboard PSLV-C60. It is made on a **180 nanometre** process and runs at about 100 megahertz, which *The Register* noted is modest by commercial standards. The point is not speed. A rocket's brain made entirely in India cannot be cut off by an export ban.
spotlights.why_it_matters: For rockets and defence, owning the chip matters more than its speed.
spotlights.memory_hook: Slow by phone standards, fast enough to fly a rocket, and Indian from design to silicon.

spotlights.name: Sanand and Dholera: India's chip plants
spotlights.spot_it: Large new industrial sheds on the flat land west of Ahmedabad, Gujarat, where the India Semiconductor Mission's first plants are rising.
spotlights.story_md: Under the **India Semiconductor Mission**, launched in 2021 with central and state subsidies, the US memory maker **Micron** opened an assembly and test plant at **Sanand**, Gujarat, on 28 February 2026. It does not make wafers: it turns DRAM and flash wafers from Micron's factories abroad into finished chips and modules. Its first shipment of made-in-India memory modules went to Dell, and the combined investment is about 2.75 billion dollars. A true wafer fab, by Tata Electronics with Taiwan's PSMC, is under construction at **Dholera**; official targets for its first chips have moved from late 2026 into 2026 to 2027.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's first step into making, not just designing, chips at scale.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sanand packs the chips; Dholera hopes to print them.

sections.title: Myths and half-truths
sections.intro_md:
Computing history is full of good stories that are not quite true. The three spotlights below cover the bug, the first computer and a quote nobody can source. Three more are worth knowing.

**Myth: more gigahertz always means a faster computer.** Clock speed is one factor. Work done per tick, the number of cores and the speed of memory matter as much. Intel's Pentium 4 had very high clock speeds in the early 2000s yet was often beaten by slower-clocked rivals, a lesson called the megahertz myth.

**Myth: computers think in ones and zeros.** Physically they handle voltages, charges and magnetic directions. One and zero are labels people and programs agree to read into them.

**Myth: Moore's law is a law of physics.** It was an observation and then a business plan. Its pace has slowed since around 2010, and the industry now gains more from clever packaging and specialised chips.

spotlights.name: The moth in the logbook
spotlights.spot_it: A brown moth taped to a page of a handwritten logbook, beside the line First actual case of bug being found.
spotlights.story_md: Operators of the Harvard Mark II, a relay computer, found a moth trapped in Relay 70 of Panel F. They taped it into the log with the note *First actual case of bug being found*. The joke is in the word actual: engineers already used bug for a fault, and Thomas Edison wrote of bugs in his inventions in 1878. Grace Hopper, who worked on the Mark II, loved telling the story and made it famous, but she did not find the moth. The page was long misdated to 1945 in popular accounts. The logbook is now in the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a real artefact attached to a false origin story.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first actual bug was funny only because bugs already existed.

spotlights.name: The Atanasoff-Berry Computer and the lawsuit
spotlights.spot_it: A desk-sized machine with a large rotating drum of capacitors and rows of vacuum tubes, rebuilt at Iowa State University.
spotlights.story_md: Physics professor **John Atanasoff** and graduate student **Clifford Berry** at Iowa State built a machine to solve systems of linear equations. It used binary numbers, vacuum tubes for logic and a rotating drum of capacitors for memory, ideas later central to computing. It was not programmable and never fully worked. In 1941 John Mauchly visited and studied it for days. In **1973**, in Honeywell v. Sperry Rand, a US federal judge ruled the ENIAC patent invalid, partly because Mauchly had derived ideas from Atanasoff. The ruling put the basic idea of the electronic digital computer in the public domain.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A court case, not a scientist, decided who invented the computer in law.
spotlights.memory_hook: A judge ruled that the computer belongs to no one.

spotlights.name: The 640K quote that was never said
spotlights.spot_it: A line passed around for decades: 640K ought to be enough for anybody, credited to Bill Gates with no source.
spotlights.story_md: The original IBM PC of 1981 could address 640 kilobytes of memory for programs, and the quote supposedly comes from that time. No one has found a recording, article or document in which Gates said it, and he has repeatedly denied it, noting that he pushed for more memory, not less. Similar quotes are just as shaky: there is no good evidence that IBM's Thomas Watson said in 1943 that the world market was maybe five computers. These lines survive because they make a neat story about short-sighted experts. A real lesson hides inside, though: memory needs grew roughly a millionfold in four decades.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Most famous computing predictions are misquotes; check before you repeat them.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nobody has ever found where Gates said 640K was enough.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
Computing is changing fast at both ends: the giant machines and the tiny switches.

**June 2026:** China's **LineShine** in Shenzhen topped the TOP500 list at 2.198 exaflops, ending El Capitan's reign; Europe's JUPITER, fifth, is the continent's first exascale machine. **29 October 2025:** Nvidia became the first company worth 5 trillion dollars, on demand for AI chips. **Late 2025:** TSMC began volume production of 2 nanometre chips with **gate-all-around** transistors, where the gate wraps the channel on every side, the first big change to the switch's shape in over a decade.

**7 October 2025:** the physics Nobel went to John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis for showing that a circuit you can hold behaves as one quantum object, the basis of superconducting quantum computers. **October 2025:** Google reported an algorithm on its Willow chip running about 13,000 times faster than the best classical method, for one specialised problem. In India, ISRO's Vikram 3201 was presented on **2 September 2025**, and Micron's Sanand plant opened on **28 February 2026**.

spotlights.name: Exascale supercomputers
spotlights.spot_it: Long rows of black cabinets in a hall at a national laboratory, cooled by water, drawing as much power as a small town.
spotlights.story_md: An **exaflop** is a billion billion calculations a second. Frontier at Oak Ridge in Tennessee was the first to pass that mark officially, in 2022. In June 2026 **LineShine** in Shenzhen became number one at 2.198 exaflops, using about 13.8 million processor cores and no GPUs, and drawing about 42 megawatts. It is the first Chinese system at the top since 2017. Every machine on the list, all 500, runs Linux. These machines simulate climate, nuclear weapons, materials and drugs, and they now also train AI. Their big limit is not chips but electricity.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The biggest computers are now limited by power stations as much as by transistors.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two quintillion sums a second, 42 megawatts of power.

spotlights.name: Quantum computers and the 2025 Nobel
spotlights.spot_it: A gold, chandelier-like cylinder of stacked plates and coiled cables: the refrigerator that cools a quantum chip to near absolute zero.
spotlights.story_md: Ordinary bits are 0 or 1. A **qubit** can be in a blend of both, and qubits can be linked so that their states depend on each other. In 1984 and 1985 at Berkeley, Clarke, Devoret and Martinis showed that a superconducting circuit could tunnel through an energy barrier and absorb energy in fixed steps, like an atom. That is the qubit Google and IBM use today; Martinis later led Google's quantum hardware. In October 2025 Google reported its Quantum Echoes result on the **Willow** chip. Useful, error-corrected quantum computers that beat classical ones on practical tasks have not yet been shown.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Quantum computers will not replace ordinary ones, but may solve some chemistry and physics problems ordinary ones cannot.
spotlights.memory_hook: A Nobel for proving a circuit can behave like an atom.

sections.title: Recap: the whole machine in one breath
sections.intro_md:
A computer is billions of switches. Each is a transistor that one voltage turns on or off. A few together make logic gates that obey Boole's algebra, as Shannon saw in 1937. Gates make adders that do arithmetic and latches that remember. Thousands of those make a processor that fetches, decodes and executes instructions to the tick of a quartz clock.

Instructions and data share memory, as the 1945 EDVAC report proposed and the Manchester Baby proved in 1948. Memory comes in layers from registers to flash, each bigger and slower. Software is layers too: machine code, compilers, operating systems, apps. Press a key, and a switch closes, a code crosses USB, the kernel hands it to an app, and a GPU paints pixels.

From Antikythera's gears and Jacquard's cards to ENIAC's tubes and a 184-billion-transistor chip, the idea stayed the same. Only the size, speed and price of the switch changed.

cards.front: What does every transistor in a chip basically do?
cards.back: Acts as a switch: on or off, read as 1 or 0.

cards.front: How many transistors are on Apple's M3 Ultra (2025)?
cards.back: 184 billion, more than the roughly 117 billion humans ever born.

cards.front: Name this 1946 machine.
cards.back: ENIAC: 17,468 vacuum tubes, about 27 tonnes, programmed with cables.

cards.front: The four things every computer does?
cards.back: Input, storage (memory), processing, output.

cards.front: Why was the stored-program idea such a big deal?
cards.back: Programs became numbers in memory, so changing the task meant loading data, not rewiring.

cards.front: The first stored program ran on the Manchester ____ on 21 June 1948.
cards.back: Baby (the Small-Scale Experimental Machine).

cards.front: Why does the Jacquard loom matter to computing?
cards.back: Its punched cards were a stored, swappable sequence of instructions: hole means lift.

cards.front: What was Ada Lovelace's big insight in 1843?
cards.back: A computing engine could manipulate any symbols, even music, not just numbers. Note G laid out a program.

cards.front: What did Shannon show in 1937?
cards.back: Switching circuits obey Boolean algebra: series is AND, parallel is OR.

cards.front: What is Turing's universal machine?
cards.back: One machine that can imitate any other given its description: the idea of software.

cards.front: The five generations of the switch?
cards.back: Relay, vacuum tube, transistor, integrated circuit, MOSFET.

cards.front: Who made the first transistor, when, where?
cards.back: Bardeen and Brattain (with Shockley's group), Bell Labs, December 1947.

cards.front: How many patterns can n bits hold?
cards.back: 2 to the power n: 8 bits give 256.

cards.front: Why is NAND special?
cards.back: It is universal: any logic, and any computer, can be built from NAND gates alone.

cards.front: The processor's endless loop?
cards.back: Fetch, decode, execute, repeat, timed by a clock.

cards.front: First commercial microprocessor, year and transistor count?
cards.back: Intel 4004, 1971, 2,300 transistors.

cards.front: Order the memory hierarchy from fastest to slowest.
cards.back: Registers, cache, DRAM, SSD, hard disk.

cards.front: What is Moore's law?
cards.back: Components on a chip double about every two years (1965, revised 1975). An observation turned into an industry plan.

cards.front: Who wrote one of the first compilers, and when?
cards.back: Grace Hopper, the A-0 system, 1952.

cards.front: Why and when did India build PARAM 8000?
cards.back: The US blocked a Cray sale in 1987; C-DAC, Pune, delivered PARAM 8000 in 1991.

cards.front: What is this, and how old?
cards.back: The Antikythera mechanism, a geared astronomical calculator, roughly 205 to 60 BCE.

cards.front: Name this 17th-century machine.
cards.back: Pascal's calculator (Pascaline), 1642.

cards.front: Whose design is this, and when was it built?
cards.back: Babbage's Difference Engine No. 2, built by the Science Museum in 1991.

cards.front: Who is this?
cards.back: Ada Lovelace, author of Note G (1843).

cards.front: Who is this?
cards.back: George Boole, The Laws of Thought (1854).

cards.front: Name this wartime machine.
cards.back: Colossus, Bletchley Park, 1944.

cards.front: What is this crude object?
cards.back: A replica of the first, point-contact transistor (Bell Labs, 1947).

cards.front: Name this chip.
What is taped into this logbook?
cards.back: The moth from the Harvard Mark II, 9 September 1947: first actual case of bug being found.

cards.front: Who is this?
cards.back: Grace Hopper, compiler pioneer and US Navy rear admiral.

cards.front: Which Indian machine is being shown here?
cards.back: TIFRAC, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Mumbai, named by Nehru.

cards.front: What is this baby picture famous for?
cards.back: The first scanned digital image, 1957: Walden Kirsch, 176 by 176 pixels.

cards.front: What is this box and keypad?
cards.back: The Apollo Guidance Computer and its DSKY.

cards.front: What kind of switch does this machine use?
cards.back: Telephone relays: it is the Zuse Z3 (replica).

cards.front: Who were the Harvard Computers?
cards.back: Women hired by Edward Pickering to classify stars on photographic plates.

cards.front: Name two of the six ENIAC programmers.
cards.back: Any of: Kathleen McNulty, Jean Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Frances Bilas, Ruth Lichterman.

cards.front: What company grew from Hollerith's census tabulator?
cards.back: IBM (renamed in 1924).

cards.front: In Boole's algebra of logic, x times x equals ____.
cards.back: x (true and true is still true).

cards.front: Kilby vs Noyce: who did what?
cards.back: Kilby (TI, 1958) made the first integrated circuit in germanium; Noyce (Fairchild, 1959) made the flat silicon chip with printed connections.

cards.front: How many characters does Unicode 17.0 (2025) hold?
Why does a watch crystal ring at 32,768 Hz?
cards.back: It is 2 to the power 15: halve it 15 times and you get one tick per second.

cards.front: How long is Grace Hopper's nanosecond?
cards.back: About 30 cm of wire: how far electricity travels in a billionth of a second.

cards.front: Why does DRAM need refreshing?
cards.back: Each bit is charge on a tiny capacitor that leaks, so it is rewritten many times a second.

cards.front: Who invented flash memory, and where did the name come from?
cards.back: Fujio Masuoka at Toshiba; erasing a whole block at once reminded a colleague of a camera flash.

cards.front: What light do the newest chip machines use, and who makes them?
cards.back: Extreme ultraviolet, 13.5 nm, from ASML in the Netherlands.

cards.front: What was new about TSMC's business model in 1987?
cards.back: It only manufactures chips designed by others: a pure foundry.

cards.front: What happens on 19 January 2038?
cards.back: A signed 32-bit count of seconds since 1 January 1970 overflows.

cards.front: What is Vikram 3201?
cards.back: ISRO SCL's indigenous 32-bit processor for launch vehicles, presented in September 2025; 180 nm, about 100 MHz.

cards.front: How are Banarasi brocade patterns stored for the loom?
cards.back: As a naksha, a graph design, punched onto a chain of Jacquard cards.

cards.front: Why is a Jacquard card chain a program?
cards.back: It is a stored sequence of binary instructions (hole or no hole) that the machine follows row by row.

quiz.prompt: What is this machine?

quiz.prompt: What did this bronze object do?
